current_answer: New firms do not automatically replace the jobs that exposed employers cut. A U.S. working-paper abstract reports that more AI-exposed existing startups reduced employment, especially in junior roles; greater entry by smaller firms left aggregate startup employment unchanged in its sample. A separate CEPR abstract reports 20% more startup formation and entry-linked labor growth in more exposed industries, while a UK abstract detects no statistically significant entry increase. These studies use different populations and measures, and none proves AI caused a net jobs gain or loss for all workers. The broad U.S. labor-market collapse claim remains unsupported; narrower entry risks remain open.

catalogue_card.question: Do more AI-era startups mean more jobs?
catalogue_card.text: Not necessarily. One U.S. study reports more startup entry but no aggregate startup-jobs gain; a UK study finds no clear entry increase. Both are exposure-based, not proof of AI causation.

summary: A U.S. startup study reports fewer jobs at more exposed existing firms, mainly junior roles; new entrants offset the loss in its aggregate startup-employment measure.
A CEPR study reports more formation and entry-linked industry labor growth, but a UK study detects no significant firm-entry increase. Different samples and outcomes prevent a clean winner.
No paper establishes a national AI-caused net jobs change or a personal career forecast.
uncertainty: The Gupta and Agarwal full papers were not inspected; abstract-level methods and uncertainty remain unverified.
The papers count different populations and endpoints; firm formation is not completed hiring.
Industry task exposure does not show actual AI use by every firm.
freshness_note: Checked 4 October 2026. Startup entry no longer appears as a stand-alone jobs counter-signal; one U.S. abstract reports flat aggregate startup employment after offsetting losses.
